regions.title: Earlier jurisdiction landmarks
regions.description: The original jurisdiction entries retain their saved locations. Their expanded source-based accounts and relationships are included in the full Civil Procedure course.

districts.title: Contacts & relatedness
districts.question: Earlier jurisdictional study notes.
principalCases: Ford Motor Co. v. Montana Eighth Judicial District Court (2021)

districts.title: Jurisdiction & forum clauses
districts.question: Earlier notes retain their original source limits.
principalCases: Carnival Cruise Lines, Inc. v. Shute

regions.title: The civil action and its legal framework
regions.description: Which court, which law, and which procedural question?
regions.routeQuestion: What is a civil action, and what governs it?

districts.title: The route through a civil action
districts.question: Civil procedure supplies the institutions, authority, notice, pleadings, party arrangements, and methods of decision through which a civil claim is heard. A favorable substantive claim still needs an appropriate court and a procedurally valid route to judgment.

districts.title: All fourteen syllabus weeks
districts.question: Read printed pages 1–29, Capron, Tickle, Pennoyer, and Article III §§ 1–2. The syllabus places the first overview before the first class. The additional pages here include the assigned case accounts and their immediate discussion.

districts.title: Separately supplied sources
districts.question: Berk v. Choy and Cross v. United States came as separate files; both are full entries with the opinion on file, and the 354-page supplement opens page by page.

regions.title: Authority over defendants
regions.description: Identify the defendant’s forum connection or another recognized basis.
regions.routeQuestion: Can this court reach the defendant?

districts.title: Territory, domicile, and personal service
districts.question: The territorial approach associated with Pennoyer linked a state court’s authority to service, consent, domicile-related settings, and property within its territory. It provides the historical starting point for the course’s personal-jurisdiction sequence.

districts.title: Claim-linked jurisdiction
districts.question: Personal jurisdiction is a court’s authority to bind a particular person or entity through its judgment. It concerns the defendant’s relationship to the forum or a separate recognized basis for submitting to that authority.
principalCases: McGee v. International Life Insurance Co. (1957)
Bristol-Myers Squibb Co. v. Superior Court (2017)

districts.title: Corporate homes and general jurisdiction
districts.question: North Carolina could not exercise all-purpose jurisdiction over foreign subsidiaries on claims arising from a bus accident in France.
principalCases: Goodyear Dunlop Tires Operations, S.A. v. Brown (2011)
Helicopteros Nacionales de Colombia, S.A. v. Hall (1984)
Perkins v. Benguet Consolidated Mining Co. (1952)

districts.title: Products and distribution
districts.question: The stream-of-commerce problem asks when a manufacturer’s distribution of a product through others supplies a sufficient connection to the state where litigation is brought. It is especially difficult when the manufacturer does not directly sell to the ultimate forum customer.
principalCases: Gray v. American Radiator & Standard Sanitary Corp. (1961)
Asahi Metal Industry Co. v. Superior Court (1987)
J. McIntyre Machinery, Ltd. v. Nicastro (2011)

districts.title: Intentional conduct and forum effects
districts.question: The effects cases examine when intentional conduct directed toward a forum supplies a jurisdictional connection even though the actor worked elsewhere. The defendant’s connection to the forum remains essential.

districts.title: Continuing contractual relationships
districts.question: A contract can create forum connections through the parties’ deliberate relationship, negotiations, future obligations, and performance. The existence of a contract with a forum resident is only part of the inquiry.

districts.title: Submission, agreements, and jurisdictional discovery
districts.question: Consent supplies a basis for personal jurisdiction through an agreement, conduct in litigation, or another legally recognized submission to the court’s authority. The assigned cases examine both how consent arises and its limits.
principalCases: Insurance Corp. of Ireland v. Compagnie des Bauxites de Guinée (1982)
Mallory v. Norfolk Southern Railway Co. (2023)
The Bremen v. Zapata Off-Shore Co. (1972)

districts.title: Online activity
districts.question: Internet-jurisdiction questions ask which online activities connect a particular defendant to a particular forum. The ability to access a site everywhere creates a need to identify meaningful forum-directed conduct.
principalCases: Zippo Manufacturing Co. v. Zippo Dot Com, Inc. (1997)

districts.title: Property-based proceedings
districts.question: Property-based jurisdiction uses a defendant’s interests in property as part of the basis for adjudication. The course distinguishes disputes about the property itself from efforts to use unrelated property to obtain leverage over a person.

districts.title: Fraud, immunity, and service
districts.question: A court may refuse to recognize service when deception procured a defendant’s presence for that purpose. The separate doctrine of immunity can protect persons present for judicial proceedings in specified circumstances.

regions.title: Notice, service, and hearing
regions.description: Explain how an affected person learns of the suit and can respond.
regions.routeQuestion: Was the defendant told, and heard?

districts.title: A reasonable method of notice
districts.question: Notice is the communication needed to give an affected person a meaningful opportunity to protect an interest before a court acts. Mullane evaluates whether the method is reasonably calculated, under the circumstances, to inform interested persons.
principalCases: Mullane v. Central Hanover Bank & Trust Co. (1950)

districts.title: Delivering the initiating papers
districts.question: Service of process is the formal delivery or legally authorized communication of the summons and complaint or equivalent initiating papers. It tells a defendant that a judicial proceeding requires a response.
principalCases: National Equipment Rental, Ltd. v. Szukhent (1964)

districts.title: Hearing before deprivation
districts.question: Due process protects persons affected by governmental adjudication through requirements of appropriate authority, notice, and an opportunity to be heard. The required protection depends on the setting and the interests at risk.

regions.title: Federal subject-matter jurisdiction
regions.description: Identify original power, related claims, and the route from state court.
regions.routeQuestion: Can a federal court hear this kind of case?

districts.title: Citizenship and diversity
districts.question: Citizenship identifies the legally relevant state or foreign affiliation of a party for diversity jurisdiction. It depends on the kind of party rather than a single universal test.

districts.title: The jurisdictional amount
districts.question: The amount in controversy is the value genuinely placed in dispute for a jurisdictional statute. It is assessed by the governing legal standard and the claim at issue, rather than simply the amount eventually awarded.

districts.title: The plaintiff’s federal claim
districts.question: Federal-question jurisdiction concerns actions arising under federal law within the applicable jurisdictional grant. Federal creation of the cause of action supplies the principal route, while a narrow category of state-law claims can also qualify.
principalCases: American Well Works Co. v. Layne & Bowler Co. (1916)
Louisville & Nashville Railroad Co. v. Mottley (1908)

districts.title: Federal issues inside state claims
districts.question: A narrow category of state-law claims can arise under federal law when resolving the claim necessarily requires deciding an actually disputed and substantial federal issue in a manner consistent with the federal-state division of judicial responsibility.
principalCases: Grable & Sons Metal Products, Inc. v. Darue Engineering & Manufacturing (2005)
Smith v. Kansas City Title & Trust Co. (1921)

districts.title: Related claims and added parties
districts.question: The pendent-party problem asks whether a related claim against or by an additional person may be heard when that person’s claim has no independent federal jurisdictional basis.
principalCases: Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Allapattah Services, Inc. (2005)
Owen Equipment & Erection Co. v. Kroger (1978)

districts.title: Removal and remand
districts.question: Removal transfers an eligible action from state court to federal court through a procedure authorized by Congress. It ordinarily depends on federal original jurisdiction and the removing party’s statutory role.
principalCases: Dart Cherokee Basin Operating Co. v. Owens (2014)
Home Depot U.S.A., Inc. v. Jackson (2019)
Lively v. Wild Oats Markets, Inc. (2006)
Shamrock Oil & Gas Corp. v. Sheets (1941)

regions.title: Venue and movement between courts
regions.description: Separate a proper location from a more suitable location.
regions.routeQuestion: Which district, and can the case move?

districts.title: The proper district
districts.question: The historical local-action rule associated certain claims involving land with courts where the land was located. The readings examine the rule’s origins, contested rationale, and later statutory treatment.
principalCases: Bates v. C & S Adjusters, Inc. (1992)

districts.title: Transfer within the federal system
districts.question: Transfer moves litigation from one federal district to another under statutory authority. Different statutes address a convenient alternative to a proper venue, an improper venue, and coordinated pretrial proceedings.
principalCases: Atlantic Marine Construction Co. v. U.S. District Court (2013)

districts.title: An alternative forum
districts.question: Forum non conveniens permits dismissal in favor of an available adequate alternative forum when the governing balance strongly favors litigation there. It often matters when transfer within the federal system cannot reach the alternative forum.

regions.title: Ascertaining the applicable law
regions.description: Identify the competing state and federal sources before selecting a test.
regions.routeQuestion: Whose law applies in federal court?

districts.title: The Erie problem
districts.question: Forum shopping is choosing a court in light of advantages that the forum’s rules, governing law, or procedures may offer. It becomes legally significant when a doctrine seeks to prevent particular incentives or unfair differences.
principalCases: Black & White Taxicab & Transfer Co. v. Brown & Yellow Taxicab & Transfer Co. (1928)

districts.title: State rights and federal judicial interests
districts.question: A limitations period restricts the time for bringing or enforcing a claim. Its procedural treatment can affect jurisdictional strategy, the Erie inquiry, amendment, and the availability of relief.
principalCases: Byrd v. Blue Ridge Rural Electric Cooperative, Inc. (1958)

districts.title: Federal provisions: scope and validity
districts.question: A scope inquiry asks whether the federal provision actually answers the disputed procedural question. A direct conflict requires a different analysis from a situation in which the state and federal provisions can operate together.
principalCases: Cohen v. Beneficial Industrial Loan Corp. (1949)
Ragan v. Merchants Transfer & Warehouse Co. (1949)
Gasperini v. Center for Humanities, Inc. (1996)
Shady Grove Orthopedic Associates, P.A. v. Allstate Insurance Co. (2010)
Stewart Organization, Inc. v. Ricoh Corp. (1988)

districts.title: Specialized federal common law
districts.question: Specialized federal common law consists of judicially developed federal rules supported by particular federal interests or authority, rather than a general power arising from federal jurisdiction.
principalCases: Clearfield Trust Co. v. United States (1943)

districts.title: State choice of law and federal rights
districts.question: Choice of law identifies which jurisdiction’s substantive law governs a claim. This is separate from whether a court has authority over the case and parties.
principalCases: Dice v. Akron, Canton & Youngstown Railroad Co. (1952)

regions.title: Modern pleading
regions.description: Move from an intelligible claim to responses, amendment, and responsible filings.
regions.routeQuestion: What must the complaint and answer say?

districts.title: What a complaint must communicate
districts.question: Notice pleading emphasizes giving the opposing party an intelligible account of the claim and its grounds without requiring the technical formulas of older pleading systems. The assigned cases trace its development and later qualifications.

districts.title: Plausibility and factual inference
districts.question: Plausibility asks whether the well-pleaded factual allegations support a reasonable inference of entitlement to relief in the context of the claim. Legal labels and recitations of elements do not supply missing facts.

districts.title: Claims requiring greater detail
districts.question: Rule 9(b) requires particular circumstances for allegations of fraud or mistake. The requirement concerns the pleaded theory, not simply the title of the statute under which the party sues.
principalCases: Tellabs, Inc. v. Makor Issues & Rights, Ltd. (2007)

districts.title: Selecting a response to the complaint
districts.question: Rule 12 provides distinct ways to respond to a complaint, including objections to authority, legal sufficiency, excessive vagueness, and specified material within the pleading. Each motion has its own purpose and preservation rules.
principalCases: Garcia v. Hilton Hotels International, Inc. (1951)

districts.title: Answers, denials, and defenses
districts.question: An answer responds to the complaint’s allegations by admitting them, denying them, or properly stating insufficient knowledge. Those responses define what remains disputed.
principalCases: Kegerise v. Susquehanna Township School District (2016)

districts.title: Changing or adding allegations and parties
districts.question: Amendment changes a party’s pleading as the case develops. The rules distinguish changes allowed without permission from those requiring consent or leave of court, and address the effect on timing and trial.

districts.title: Responsibility for filings
districts.question: Certification and verification requirements attach responsibility to statements submitted to the court. Sanctions can enforce that responsibility but require the applicable substantive standard and procedural protections.

regions.title: Joinder and coordinated litigation
regions.description: Identify who claims against whom, the procedural device, and independent authority.
regions.routeQuestion: Who and what can be joined in one action?

districts.title: Who holds the asserted right?
districts.question: The real party in interest is the person entitled under the governing substantive law to enforce the right asserted. The inquiry can change when rights are assigned or an insurer becomes subrogated to a claim.
principalCases: Ellis Canning Co. v. International Harvester Co. (1953)

districts.title: Combining claims
districts.question: Joinder determines which claims and persons can be included in one action. Different devices govern multiple claims, counterclaims, crossclaims, additional defendants, required parties, interpleader, and intervention.

districts.title: Claims against an opponent
districts.question: A counterclaim is a claim against an opposing party. Rule 13 distinguishes compulsory claims arising from the relevant transaction or occurrence from permissive claims that may be asserted without that connection.
principalCases: United States ex rel. D’Agostino Excavators, Inc. v. Heyward-Robinson Co. (1970)

districts.title: Claims against a coparty
districts.question: A crossclaim is a claim against a coparty, such as one defendant’s claim against another defendant. Rule 13(g) requires the specified connection to the transaction, occurrence, or property involved in the action.
principalCases: LASA Per L’Industria Del Marmo Societa Per Azioni v. Alexander (1969)

districts.title: Adding named parties and managing trials
districts.question: A court can coordinate related litigation or separate issues for trial without treating every procedural unit as one merged claim. These management choices seek efficiency while limiting prejudice and confusion.

districts.title: Protecting an absent person
districts.question: A judgment ordinarily does not bind a person who was neither a party nor represented through a recognized exception. Yet litigation can still practically impair an absentee’s interests even without formally binding that person.
principalCases: Bank of California National Ass’n v. Superior Court (1940)
Provident Tradesmens Bank & Trust Co. v. Patterson (1968)
Republic of the Philippines v. Pimentel (2008)

districts.title: Potential liability over
districts.question: Impleader brings a nonparty into an action because that person may owe the defending party all or part of the liability asserted by the plaintiff. Common examples involve indemnity or contribution.

districts.title: Competing demands on a fund
districts.question: Statutory interpleader is a specific federal jurisdictional route for competing claims to money or property. The readings distinguish its minimal-diversity, fund, service, venue, and injunction provisions from ordinary Rule 22 interpleader.
principalCases: Hancock Oil Co. v. Independent Distributing Co. (1944)
Pan American Fire & Casualty Co. v. Revere (1960)
State Farm Fire & Casualty Co. v. Tashire (1967)

districts.title: Entering an existing action
districts.question: Intervention is a procedure by which a person outside the lawsuit seeks to enter it to protect an interest or participate under the rule’s conditions. Rule 24 distinguishes intervention of right from permissive intervention.

districts.title: Coordination without automatic merger
districts.question: Multidistrict litigation coordinates federal actions pending in different districts that share common factual questions. Under § 1407, the Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation can transfer them for coordinated or consolidated pretrial proceedings.
principalCases: Lexecon Inc. v. Milberg Weiss Bershad Hynes & Lerach (1998)

regions.title: Class actions
regions.description: Representation, certification, notice, settlement, and the effect on absentees.
regions.routeQuestion: When can one suit bind a class?

districts.title: Representation of absentees
districts.question: Adequate representation protects absentees by requiring representatives and counsel capable of pursuing the class’s interests without disqualifying conflicts. It is central to the legitimacy of binding people who do not appear individually.

districts.title: Proof supporting certification
districts.question: Certification is the court’s decision that a proposed group and its representatives satisfy the legal conditions for class treatment. It requires analysis of the applicable Rule 23 requirements, not simply acceptance of a class label.

districts.title: Notice and the exclusion choice
districts.question: Class notice informs absentees about the action, their rights, and the effect of participating or remaining in the class. The required method and opportunity to opt out depend on the category and procedural stage.

districts.title: Settlements and conflicts within the class
districts.question: A limited-fund class addresses a situation where separate claims could exhaust a genuinely insufficient fund and impair other claimants’ recovery. Mandatory treatment requires strong justification because class members lack the ordinary damages-class opt-out choice.

districts.title: Authority to hear the class claims
districts.question: Absent plaintiff class members do not face the same burdens as defendants compelled to defend, and the assigned cases protect them through the structure of representation and procedural safeguards.
principalCases: Standard Fire Insurance Co. v. Knowles (2013)

districts.title: The scope of the resulting judgment
districts.question: Issue preclusion prevents relitigation of a qualifying issue actually litigated and necessarily determined in an earlier action. It differs from a broader bar on relitigating the same claim.
principalCases: Cooper v. Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond (1984)

districts.title: Individual arbitration and class waivers
districts.question: A class waiver restricts the use of representative or aggregate proceedings, often through an agreement requiring individual arbitration. Its effect can depend on federal arbitration law and the applicable contract defenses.

regions.title: Summary judgment
regions.description: Connect the evidence, burdens, and permissible factfinding.
regions.routeQuestion: Can the case end before trial?

districts.title: Historical development and competing concerns
districts.question: The assigned history traces movement from narrow collection procedures and cautious use toward the broader role associated with the 1986 trilogy. Competing concerns involve unnecessary trials, jury protection, cost, and access to proof.
principalCases: Poller v. Columbia Broadcasting System, Inc. (1962)

districts.title: The motion and the response
districts.question: A claim passes through different tests as litigation proceeds. Pleading concerns sufficient allegations; the production burden concerns enough evidence for a reasonable verdict; persuasion concerns whether the factfinder is convinced under the governing standard.
principalCases: Adickes v. S. H. Kress & Co. (1970)

districts.title: Reasonable inferences and the trial burden
districts.question: An inference is a conclusion drawn from evidence about an unobserved or disputed fact. At summary judgment, reasonable favorable inferences belong to the nonmovant, while credibility and weight generally remain for trial.
principalCases: Matsushita Electric Industrial Co. v. Zenith Radio Corp. (1986)
